title: Human Blockheads: A Real Thing
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the human blockhead stunt, in which a performer drives a nail or similar object up the nose and into the nasal cavity, creating the illusion of hammering it into the skull. They cover the stunt's history, starting with Melvin Burkhart, a sideshow talker and performer who popularized it in the West after Robert Ripley took him on, and who reportedly got the idea after boxing-related bone removal from his nose. They explain skull and nose anatomy (the nose is mostly cartilage, with a hollow nasal cavity leading back to the nasopharynx), how the illusion works, the difficulty of overcoming the sneeze reflex, safety warnings, modern performer Ryan Stock and his meat hook stunt, and the faith healer John of God's forceps procedure, which skeptic James Randi exposed. The episode opens with banter about glasses and a San Francisco Sketch Fest show, and closes with listener mail about young children and advertising.

segments.title: Sketch Fest plug, glasses, and opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts promote a San Francisco Sketch Fest show, then chat about new glasses prescriptions and childhood memories of wearing glasses.

segments.title: Defining the human blockhead stunt
segments.summary: The hosts define a human blockhead as a performer who pushes a nail or similar sharp object up the nose, and distinguish a stunt from a trick. They discuss misconceptions that the object enters the skull through a hole.

segments.title: Piercings, medical holes, and Stelarc
segments.summary: The hosts mention body modification and holes, including medical reasons for new openings and the performance artist Stelarc's ear grafted onto his arm.

segments.title: Melvin Burkhart and the origin of the human blockhead
segments.summary: Melvin Burkhart, a sideshow talker and performer, accidentally got a nail through his nose as a teenager and later built an act around it. Robert Ripley discovered him and reportedly coined the name human blockhead. A Todd Robbins quote credits Burkhart, and the hosts note earlier Hindu street performers may have done similar stunts.

segments.title: Burkhart's boxing injury and nasal bone removal
segments.summary: Burkhart reportedly had bone removed from around his nasal cavity after a boxing injury, which he believed made his nasal passage larger and inspired the act after doctors inserted instruments in his nose. Henny Youngman is mentioned as his doctor.

segments.title: Skull, nose cartilage, and nasal cavity anatomy
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the skull is made of many bones, the nose is mostly cartilage, and behind the nose is a hollow nasal cavity that runs back to the nasopharynx. Conchae grooves keep the passage moist.

segments.title: How the illusion works and performer technique
segments.summary: The nasal opening appears to point upward but really leads backward, which creates the illusion. Performers slide the nail along the floor of the nasal cavity and use a hammer and sound effects to fake the impact. The hosts warn against attempting it and cite advice to learn from experienced performers.

segments.title: Sneeze reflex and training
segments.summary: Overcoming the sneeze reflex is the biggest challenge. The hosts explain the reflex arc and how a sneeze works, then describe how performers train by repeatedly stimulating the reflex with a Q-tip, and how they clean their nails and avoid infection.

segments.title: Ryan Stock and the human meat hook stunt
segments.summary: Ryan Stock is a modern performer known for a human meat hook stunt in which a hook goes through the nose and out the mouth, and he set a record for pulling a heavy car. The hosts also discuss nasal gum and nosebleed-like anecdotes.

segments.title: John of God and psychic surgery exposed by James Randi
segments.summary: The hosts describe Brazilian faith healer John of God, who uses forceps up the nose as a visible procedure. James Randi exposed it as similar to the blockhead trick. The hosts mention possible future episodes on faith healing and psychic surgery.

segments.title: Resources and sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts suggest further resources on human blockheads and credit sources, then mention upcoming holiday wishes and a birthday shout-out.

segments.title: Listener mail on advertising to kids
segments.summary: A listener from Northern Virginia describes her 18-month-old recognizing Mickey Mouse on a water tower at Walt Disney World, prompting concern about advertising's influence. Another listener notes that her nearly five-year-old fast-forwards through commercials. The hosts close with contact information.
